title: Cohort resilience: scenarios & mitigation recipes (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:

This document collects pragmatic failure scenarios and operational "recipes" for protecting user cohorts during staged rollouts (canaries, microreleases, A/B). It is a working sprint artifact: testable mitigation patterns, signal-to-action mappings, and cheap simulation ideas we can run in the rollout sandboxes. The goal is not to enumerate every failure mode but to give on-call and rollout stewards a small, high-confidence playbook they can apply without second-guessing.

Quick context notes to self:
- This is product+ops-facing, intended to augment the existing rollout-runbook with cohort-level mitigation patterns.
- Focus on stability-first: preserve availability and predictable latency for the baseline cohort while still collecting readable signals on the variant.
- Keep recipes short: trigger -> short diagnosis -> mitigation -> post-mortem checklist.

High-level failure categories (observed in prior experiments):
1) Latency amplification in tail percentiles after routing small cohorts to heavier models or different hardware (p99- p999 spikes).
2) Output quality regressions that materially increase human review or complaint rate for specific user slices (regional dialects, enterprise workflows).
3) Cost shock from runaway token churn (looping prompts, longer outputs, error retries).
4) Traffic partition imbalance leading to cascade backpressure in downstream services (embedding/rerankers).
5) Telemetry blindspots: sampling or trace gaps that make root cause ambiguous for microcohorts.

Signal-to-action patterns (compact):
- Signal: sustained p99 latency > baseline+200ms for 2+ minutes (cohort-specific).
  Action: auto-failover policy -> reroute cohort to baseline model variant (10s DNS TTL fallback) and notify steward via #rollout-alerts.
  Why: short window avoids noisy flapping; automated fallback protects baseline SLA.

- Signal: quality metric delta (BLEU/EMB-sim/RR) drops > 5% on validation prompts for cohort over 300 requests.
  Action: pause exposure, increase human-eval sampling to 100 examples, and trigger canary-rollback-if-regression persists after manual triage.
  Why: preserve user trust and create human-in-the-loop guardrails for ambiguous model regressions.

- Signal: token consumption rate > projected by >40% for > 10 minutes.
  Action: throttle throughput for variant to 50% of original weight, enable max_tokens cap at 256, flag billing alert and open incident stub.
  Why: contain cost while preserving partial functionality.

- Signal: downstream queue length rising > X (queue threshold depends on service).
  Action: shift cohort to edge-cached responses (if available) or reduce variant weight to 0% with graceful fallback to baseline responses.
  Why: prevent cascade failures and preserve downstream SLAs.

Mitigation recipes (step-by-step)
Recipe A — "Fast tail mitigation" (latency spikes)
1) Detect: cohort p99 > baseline+200ms for 2 samples of 30s windows.
2) Quick triage: check GPU/host SRE dashboard and model throughput metric; see if batching increased or kernel fallback occurred.
3) Automated action: route cohort to an alternate compatible quantized variant (config: fallback_model=redwood-model-quant-v2) for up to 15 minutes.
4) Human step: steward inspects logs and KV cache hit rate; if KV cache < 40% for cohort prefix, consider configured prefix caching adjustment.
5) Post-action: run small synthetic workload (10k synth queries) in canary sandbox to validate.

Recipe B — "Quality degradation quarantine"
1) Detect: eval set score delta > threshold for cohort.
2) Immediate: pause ramp for the cohort and mark cohort as 'quarantined' in rollout metadata.
3) Triage: attach manual label with top-3 failing prompts and model outputs, route to ML-owner.
4) If confirmed regression: rollback to previous model pin and schedule a postmortem.

Recipe C — "Cost surge containment"
1) Detect: token burn rate > forecast by 40% and projected monthly overage.
2) Action: set per-request token cap and enable response truncation policy; reduce cohort weight to 10%.
3) Notify finance+owner and instantiate a cost-watch incident channel.

Simulation and rehearsal plan (cheap experiments to validate recipes)
- Synthetic traffic generator: small python harness that replays real request traces with controlled prompt variations. Goal: reproduce token-churn and p99 amplification locally.
- Fault injection: artificially increase model sequence length via test prompts to validate truncation and throttle behavior.
- Canary ghosting: emulate cohort with toggled traffic weight but route to identical baseline service to validate telemetry isolation and alerting accuracy.

Observability checklist (what our dashboards should show per cohort)
- Traffic weight and absolute qps.
- Latency histograms by decile and 99/999 percentiles.
- Token consumption per request distribution and 95th quantile.
- KV cache hit rate, prefix match rate.
- Downstream queue lengths and error rates (reranker/embedding).
- Human-eval sample fail-rate and sample-level diffs.
- Rollout metadata: steward, hypothesis, linked PR/flag, canary start time.

Escalation and stakeholder comms templates (short)
- Slack subject line: "[Rollout Alert] cohort=<name> p99 up >200ms — auto-fallback enacted"
- Minimal body: "Auto-fallback activated for cohort <name> at <time>. Baseline path restored. Link to dashboard: <url>. Steward: @Maya. Next step: triage in 20m."

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs (notes)
- What is the right time window for quality signals vs noisy short blips? (2m vs 10m?)
- How do we balance human eval frequency with cost for small cohorts?
- Should some cohorts (high-value enterprise) be excluded from auto-fallback and require manual steward approval?
- Need a clearer mapping from product SLAs to numeric thresholds we use in the runbook.

Next actionable tasks (short backlog)
- Build the synthetic traffic harness and attach to rollout-sim pipeline (ENG-8421).
- Add cohort-level p99 view to the main rollout dashboard with slice filtering (data-visibility).
- Draft a short-run training doc for oncall and stewards with 3 example incidents and how recipes apply.

References and quick links:
- Confluence: Cohort Resilience Index (linked above).
- Jira: ENG-8421 (synthetic-sim), OPS-119 (fallback automation).
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/rollout-sim/pull/67

Notes to self: keep this lightweight and runnable in the next sprint. After 2 rehearsals with the simulation harness, move recipes into the canonical runbook and mark status to in_review.

End of draft.
